text: What should the CTO ask vendors about airline disruption recovery AI?
claudePromptBoundary: Full production prompt is reconstructed from current source template and captured source packet. ai_egress_audit stores prompt hash/snapshot refs, not raw prompt text by default.
claudeResponse:
Airline Demo's CTO should walk into any disruption recovery AI vendor conversation with five hard questions — and the answers will separate credible vendors from ones selling a demo. First, ask how the model handles crew legality constraints in real time. Crew recovery is where most airline AI fails in production.
If the vendor can't show live integration with a crew legality feed and explain how rule violations are blocked before a recommendation surfaces, the product isn't production-ready for Airline Demo's environment. Second, ask what the model does when data is stale.
Airline Demo's IROPS value chain depends on eight live feeds — flight status, tail assignment, crew availability, PNR events, gate turn events, and more. Ask the vendor to specify the maximum tolerable data lag for each input before model confidence degrades, and whether the system alerts the operator or silently degrades.
Third, ask where the human sits in the loop. For any decision touching crew or passengers, Airline Demo's control framework requires human-in-loop approval until model-risk tiering is signed off. Ask the vendor to show the override log, the escalation path, and how the audit trail is maintained.
If they can't demo that, it's not compliant with Airline Demo's AI governance posture. Fourth, ask how recovery decisions are sequenced across aircraft, crew, and passengers simultaneously. IROPS isn't three separate problems — it's one constrained optimization where a crew swap affects a gate turn, which affects a passenger connection.
